name: The Private Language Argument
statement: A language only you could understand is impossible: meaning needs a public standard of correctness.
statementAccent: meaning needs a public standard of correctness
meaning: The private language argument is Ludwig Wittgenstein's argument, in his Philosophical Investigations of 1953, especially the sections from 243 to around 315, against the possibility of a private language: a language that could in principle be understood only by a single person, whose words refer to that person's immediate private sensations, knowable only to them, so that no one else could understand it. Wittgenstein argues that such a language is impossible. The target is the Cartesian and empiricist picture on which words for sensations, like pain, get their meaning by each person privately associating the word with an inner experience available only to them, a private ostensive definition. Against this, Wittgenstein's central argument, in section 258, uses the example of a diarist who tries to name a recurring private sensation S and to write S in a diary whenever it recurs. Wittgenstein argues that there is no criterion of correctness for using S the same way again, no distinction between correctly applying S and merely seeming to apply it correctly, so that, as he puts it, whatever is going to seem right to me is right, which only means that here we cannot talk about right. Without a criterion of correctness there is no genuine rule-following and hence no meaning. The famous beetle-in-a-box passage, section 293, reinforces the point that the reference of sensation words is not a private inner object.
mechanism: The argument works by showing that a would-be private language lacks the conditions necessary for meaning. Meaning a word by an expression requires that there be a difference between using it correctly and merely thinking one is using it correctly; genuine rule-following demands a standard of correctness independent of one's mere impression of correctness. In the diarist example of section 258, someone undertakes to give a name, S, to a sensation available only to them and to record each recurrence. But when the moment comes to apply S again, there is nothing that could count as getting it right as opposed to merely seeming to get it right, because the only check available is the diarist's own present inclination, which cannot be both the thing being tested and the test. Wittgenstein concludes that here we cannot speak of correctness at all, and so cannot speak of meaning: a sign with no possible criterion of correct application is not a word with a meaning. The beetle-in-a-box passage of section 293 dramatizes a related point: imagine everyone has a box containing something they call a beetle, but no one can look into anyone else's box. If the word beetle had a use in the shared language, the thing in the box would drop out of consideration as irrelevant; the private object cancels out, and the public use of the word is what carries its meaning. The moral is that meaning depends on public criteria and rules embedded in a shared practice, a form of life, rather than on private inner ostension. Wittgenstein denied this made him a behaviorist, insisting a sensation is not a something, but not a nothing either.

examples.text: A diarist naming a private sensation S has no criterion of correctness for reapplying it, so whatever seems right is right, and correctness collapses.
If each person had a private beetle no one else could see, the object drops out as irrelevant to the word's public use.
Wittgenstein denied he was denying sensations, saying a sensation is not a something, but not a nothing either.

variants.name: The criterion of correctness
variants.text: The requirement that meaning needs a distinction between being right and merely seeming right, which a private language cannot supply.

variants.name: Kripke's rule-following reading
variants.text: Saul Kripke's 1982 interpretation tying the argument to a skeptical paradox about meaning and a community solution.

whyItMatters: The private language argument is one of the most discussed and influential arguments in twentieth-century philosophy, striking at a picture of the mind and meaning that had dominated modern thought since Descartes and the empiricists. By arguing that a language whose words name only private, inner sensations is impossible, Wittgenstein undercut the assumption that meaning is essentially a private mental affair, that each of us first grasps our own sensations and then attaches words to them by inner ostension. In its place he put a picture of meaning as public, rule-governed, and rooted in shared practices and forms of life, a picture that reoriented the philosophy of language and mind. The argument bears directly on the problem of other minds, on debates about the nature of sensation and introspection, and on the whole issue of rule-following, which Saul Kripke made central with his 1982 reading of Wittgenstein, drawing out a skeptical paradox about what fixes the meaning of our words and a communitarian response to it. Whether one accepts the argument or contests its structure, and its exact structure and conclusion remain much debated, it forces a reckoning with the idea that meaning could be a private possession. As the case against a purely private language, it is a landmark of modern philosophy.

working.text: imagine trying to name a sensation only you can experience, by a private inner ostension.
ask what could distinguish using the word correctly from merely seeming to, and find no criterion of correctness.
conclude that without a public criterion there is no rule-following and so no meaning, and that meaning requires shared practice.

limits: The private language argument is powerful but its exact structure and conclusion are genuinely contested, and there is a large interpretive literature rather than a single agreed reconstruction. Commentators disagree over whether Wittgenstein shows that a private language is false or that it is strictly nonsensical, over precisely which conception of privacy is the target, and over how the argument relates to the surrounding rule-following considerations. Saul Kripke's influential 1982 reading, sometimes called Kripkenstein, recasts the material as a general skeptical paradox about meaning with a community-based solution, but many scholars dispute whether this is faithful to Wittgenstein. A persistent worry is whether the argument collapses into behaviorism by seeming to deny inner sensations, a charge Wittgenstein explicitly rejected, insisting that a sensation is not a something but not a nothing either. Precise section numbers and quotations, such as 258, 293, and 304, and translations that render the key phrase as right or as correct, reward care. So the private language argument robustly ties meaning to public criteria of correctness, understood as a deep but interpretively contested argument whose reconstruction and even its conclusion remain debated.
misreadings: The private language argument is not the claim that we cannot have private sensations or keep our thoughts to ourselves; it targets a language whose words could in principle be understood by only one person. It is not a denial that sensations exist, which would be behaviorism Wittgenstein rejected, but a claim about what meaning requires. And it does not merely say that no one else happens to understand such a language, but that it could not have meaning at all for lack of a criterion of correctness, so treating it as banning private thoughts, as denying sensations, or as a claim about mere contingent secrecy, misreads the argument.
origin: Ludwig Wittgenstein's argument in the Philosophical Investigations (1953), around sections 243 to 315, that a language whose words name only private sensations is impossible because meaning requires public criteria of correctness.
